title: Python 3: Zero to Production Engineering
subtitle: From object references to tested APIs and safe IT automation.

chapters.title: Python syntax, variables & the memory model
chapters.summary: Understand names, objects, mutability and predictable functions.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Names refer to objects
Python assignment binds a name to an object. It does not automatically copy the object. When two names point at one list, a mutation through either name changes the same list. Rebinding a name points it elsewhere. This distinction explains many production bugs in configuration and request handling.

## Build a mental trace
Before running the example, draw the names and the lists they reference. A slice makes a shallow copy: its outer list is separate, but nested mutable objects can still be shared. Use a deliberate deep copy only when nested independence is required.

## Defaults and input boundaries
Function default arguments are evaluated when the function is defined. Use `None` as a sentinel when each invocation needs a fresh list. At an API boundary, convert and validate external values instead of assuming every input is an integer. Handle a specific exception and return a useful error; swallowing every exception can hide a broken dependency.

## Engineering exercise
Write a function that accepts an optional list of ticket IDs and returns a new list containing one additional ID. Verify that the caller's list is unchanged. Then test an empty list, repeated calls, and an invalid input. Document whether the function mutates its arguments.

codeSnippet.code:
tickets = ["INC-1"]
shared = tickets
separate = tickets.copy()
shared.append("INC-2")
print(len(tickets), len(separate))

keyTakeaways: Assignment binds names; it does not clone objects.
A shallow copy still shares nested objects.
Use None for a fresh mutable default.

conceptChecks.question: What does a = b do when b is a list?
options: Binds a to the same list
conceptChecks.explanation: Assignment shares the reference; it is not a copy.

conceptChecks.question: Which default avoids sharing a list between calls?
conceptChecks.explanation: Allocate a new list in the function when the argument is None.

chapters.title: Data structures & comprehensions
chapters.summary: Choose structures by the operations your application needs.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Match the structure to the job
Use a list for an ordered sequence, a dictionary for key-to-value lookups, and a set for membership and deduplication. A tuple can represent a fixed group of values, but a tuple containing a list is not deeply immutable. Dictionary keys must be hashable; a mutable list cannot be a dictionary key.

## Transform data clearly
A comprehension is useful when the transformation and filter fit in one readable expression. Separate validation, network I/O and exception handling into named functions. A clever nested comprehension can obscure which records were rejected and why.

## Preserve meaning while deduplicating
A set removes duplicates but does not promise an application-specific order. If first-seen order matters, maintain an output list and a seen set, or use dictionary insertion order deliberately. Never rely on incidental iteration order for deterministic test expectations.

## Engineering exercise
Given incident dictionaries with an ID, priority and owner, build an owner-to-open-count index. Reject records missing required keys, preserve the original data, and test repeated owners. Discuss the memory trade-off between building a complete list and processing an iterator one record at a time.
keyTakeaways: Use a dict for indexed lookup and a set for membership.
Keep comprehensions short enough to review.
Choose explicit ordering when order matters.

conceptChecks.question: Which structure directly models unique ticket IDs?
conceptChecks.explanation: A set represents distinct hashable values.

conceptChecks.question: What does counts.get(key, 0) provide?
options: A default for a missing key
conceptChecks.explanation: dict.get returns the supplied default when the key is absent.

chapters.title: Functions, decorators, generators & AsyncIO
chapters.summary: Separate pure transformations from asynchronous I/O.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Small functions have clear contracts
A useful function states its input, output, mutation behavior and failure modes. Keep a pure transformation separate from file or network access so it can be tested without an external service. A decorator wraps a callable; preserve metadata with `functools.wraps` when building one.

## Streams and suspension
A generator yields values on demand rather than constructing a complete result list. This reduces peak memory when the consumer processes values incrementally. It does not make CPU work parallel. Exhausted generators cannot simply be replayed without creating a new iterator.

## Cooperative concurrency
An async function returns a coroutine until awaited or scheduled. Tasks cooperate at suspension points. Blocking I/O inside the event loop can stall unrelated tasks; use an async client or move suitable blocking work off the loop. Add timeouts, cancellation handling and concurrency bounds before calling many external systems.

## Engineering exercise
Design a bounded incident-enrichment worker. Keep ID normalization synchronous and pure, fetch metadata asynchronously, and return a per-item success or error. Define what happens when one dependency times out. Avoid launching thousands of unbounded tasks merely because the API is asynchronous.

codeSnippet.code:
import asyncio

async def label(value):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return value.upper()

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(label("euc"), label("cloud"))
    print(", ".join(results))

asyncio.run(main())

keyTakeaways: Await or schedule coroutines deliberately.
Generators are lazy, not automatically parallel.
Bound concurrency and define cancellation behavior.

conceptChecks.question: What can stall an AsyncIO event loop?
options: Calling blocking I/O directly in a coroutine
conceptChecks.explanation: Blocking work prevents other tasks from running on that loop.

conceptChecks.question: What does yield enable?
conceptChecks.explanation: A generator yields values incrementally to its consumer.

chapters.title: OOP, type hints & packaging
chapters.summary: Make code understandable to humans, tools and deployment systems.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Model behavior, not just containers
A class is useful when state and behavior belong together. Composition often produces a simpler design than a deep inheritance tree: inject a notification client into a ticket service instead of inheriting networking behavior. Dataclasses reduce boilerplate for plain data while explicit methods protect invariants.

## Types are a contract, not a security boundary
Type hints help static analysis and editors, but normal Python execution does not enforce them automatically. Validate untrusted JSON at runtime. Use a small protocol or interface boundary so a test double can replace a network client without importing the real service.

## Reproducible delivery
Use a virtual environment and project metadata such as `pyproject.toml`. Separate runtime dependencies from development tooling. Pin or lock the dependency set used by deployment, record the supported Python version, and build in CI. Do not commit API keys or depend on an import that works only because your terminal happens to be in the source folder.

## Engineering exercise
Package a ticket normalization module with one public function and tests. Install it into a clean environment, import it from outside its repository directory, and run the tests. This exposes accidental reliance on local paths.

codeSnippet.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Ticket:
    id: str
    priority: int

ticket = Ticket("INC-9", 2)
print(f"{ticket.id}: P{ticket.priority}")

keyTakeaways: Type hints do not replace runtime validation.
Prefer composition for replaceable dependencies.
Test installation in a clean environment.

conceptChecks.question: Do type hints alone validate incoming JSON at runtime?
conceptChecks.explanation: Static annotations are not automatic runtime validation.

conceptChecks.question: Why inject a client into a service?
conceptChecks.explanation: Dependency injection makes boundaries replaceable and testable.

chapters.title: FastAPI, pytest & safe automation
chapters.summary: Ship a small API with validation, tests and operational limits.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Separate the HTTP boundary
FastAPI can validate request models and generate an API schema. Keep business logic outside route handlers: the route should translate a validated request into a service call and map expected failures into useful responses. Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that identity can act on a particular ticket.

## Test behavior at the boundary
Use pytest assertions for both happy paths and failures. Include missing fields, invalid values, unauthorized users and dependency timeouts. A test that repeats the implementation's calculation can miss the same bug. Prefer independently chosen examples with explicit expected results.

## Treat automation as a transaction
An IT automation endpoint should define an idempotency key, audit event and approval rule before changing external state. Retrying a request must not repeatedly disable an account or extend a subscription. Use dry-run previews and least-privilege credentials. Background work needs bounded retries and a way to inspect failure.

## Production exercise
Design a ticket-priority endpoint with a documented schema, one pure decision function and an injected repository. Add a health endpoint that does not expose credentials, configure request timeouts, and test that an unauthorized user cannot modify another team's ticket.
keyTakeaways: Test authorization and failure paths as well as successful responses.
Use idempotency for retried side effects.
Validate requests before calling business logic.

title: AI Engineering with GitHub Copilot & LLMs
subtitle: Build with context, test the boundaries, and ship responsible AI features.

chapters.title: Prompt engineering & context windows
chapters.summary: Specify constraints, evidence and acceptance criteria.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Define the task before asking for code
A useful coding prompt includes the current behavior, desired behavior, architectural constraints and a way to verify success. Add relevant interfaces and examples rather than dumping an entire repository. Tell the assistant which files or contracts must remain compatible.

## Context is a finite working set
A model can only use the context supplied to it within its limits. A large conversation can crowd out an important constraint. Keep a concise task summary and refresh it when requirements change. Treat generated statements about unseen files as hypotheses to verify against the actual repository.

## Data is not an instruction
Retrieved documents, ticket text and repository comments can contain malicious instructions. A tool-using system must keep trusted system rules separate from untrusted content. Do not place credentials in prompts, and do not allow a document to grant itself permission to run commands.

## Engineering exercise
Write a prompt for adding an authenticated ticket endpoint. Include input/output examples, organization scoping, error behavior and tests. Then ask the assistant to identify missing information before editing. Review the resulting diff against each acceptance criterion instead of deciding solely from a confident explanation.

codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Task: Add ticket search
Checks: organization scope, SQL parameters, pagination

keyTakeaways: Give concrete constraints and acceptance examples.
Verify claims against source files.
Treat retrieved instructions as untrusted data.

conceptChecks.question: Which prompt is easiest to verify?
options: Add paginated org-scoped search; test forbidden cross-org reads
conceptChecks.explanation: Explicit behavior and checks make the result reviewable.

conceptChecks.question: A retrieved document asks the agent to reveal its token. What should happen?
options: Ignore the instruction and protect the token
Forward the token to all users
conceptChecks.explanation: Retrieved text cannot authorize disclosure or override trusted rules.

chapters.title: Completions, chat & multi-file changes
chapters.summary: Choose a workflow and keep each diff reviewable.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Use the smallest effective interaction
Inline completion is useful for a small local continuation. Chat helps explain a function, compare designs or plan a change. A multi-file editing workflow can coordinate a feature across an API and UI, but a larger edit still needs a clear boundary and review. Product names and UI locations evolve; learn the workflow rather than memorizing one button position.

## Give relevant repository context
Start from the real handler, type and test files. Ask the assistant to follow existing error shapes and dependency choices. If a feature needs a migration, configuration or deployment step, keep those visible in the change description. A green frontend build does not prove that the backend route is deployed.

## Review as an engineer
Read each changed file, especially permissions, SQL, dependency updates and generated configuration. Run the project's checks. If the assistant introduces a second authentication system into an already working app, correct the architectural mismatch before building more UI.

## Engineering exercise
Implement a read-only search filter in one small change. Then add the API parameter in a second step with a matching integration test. Compare the diffs and explain how each step can be rolled back.
keyTakeaways: Keep multi-file changes bounded by a contract.
Review permissions and configuration explicitly.
Check frontend and backend deployment independently.

conceptChecks.question: A multi-file edit compiles. What is still needed?
options: Review the diff and run behavior/security checks
conceptChecks.explanation: Compilation checks types and syntax, not every behavioral or access rule.

conceptChecks.question: Which context is most useful for an API change?
options: The handler, request types and relevant tests
conceptChecks.explanation: Related source contracts guide a compatible implementation.

chapters.title: AI-assisted tests, refactoring & security review
chapters.summary: Use independent expectations and adversarial cases.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Ask for tests that can fail meaningfully
A useful test describes externally observable behavior. Provide cases with independent expected results, including invalid input and unauthorized callers. Generated tests can accidentally repeat the same mistake as generated code, so choose examples yourself and inspect what the assertions actually prove.

## Refactor behind a stable contract
Capture current behavior before moving responsibilities. Small extractions make it easier to distinguish a behavior change from a mechanical reorganization. Avoid combining a broad rename, a dependency upgrade and a security change in one opaque patch.

## Security review is more than pattern matching
Ask where identity comes from, where access is checked, and whether one user's identifiers can reach another user's data. Trace the full path from request to database. Parameterized SQL addresses injection in values, but it does not automatically add tenant scoping or validate which columns a user may update.

## Engineering exercise
Give an assistant a route that updates a ticket by ID alone. Ask it to propose an authorization regression test first. Then require a scoped lookup and test that both unknown IDs and forbidden IDs return an appropriate non-leaking response.
keyTakeaways: Test denial paths and cross-account identifiers.
Parameterized values do not replace authorization.
Refactor in steps with a stable contract.

conceptChecks.question: What can a generated test accidentally do?
conceptChecks.explanation: A mirrored algorithm can produce the same wrong result in code and test.

conceptChecks.question: Parameterized SQL alone prevents which problem?
conceptChecks.explanation: Parameterized values prevent value interpolation; scope still needs explicit checks.

chapters.title: RAG pipelines & agentic workflows
chapters.summary: Retrieve permitted evidence before generating answers.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Retrieval adds evidence, not certainty
A retrieval-augmented generation pipeline chunks documents, indexes them, retrieves candidates and sends selected passages to a model. Store document identifiers and version metadata so an answer can cite the material it actually used. Similarity ranking does not prove that a passage is accurate or applicable.

## Apply access rules before context assembly
Scope retrieval to the caller's permitted organization and documents. Filtering only after generation is too late: restricted content has already reached the model. Avoid mixing private and public caches, and include identity or policy scope in cache keys.

## Agents need bounded authority
An agent can select tools and iterate, but each tool must verify its own authorization. Limit the number of steps, cost and time. For actions such as changing an account or sending a message, provide a reviewable preview and an approval boundary. A natural-language suggestion should not silently become a privileged command.

## Engineering exercise
Sketch a knowledge search endpoint. Include document-level permissions, a retrieval limit, citations, and an explicit no-evidence response. Test a user asking for a document they cannot read and a retrieved passage containing an instruction to ignore the access policy.

codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Retrieve permitted documents → assemble context → cite evidence

keyTakeaways: Enforce document permissions before retrieval reaches the model.
Preserve citations and document versions.
Bound tool authority, cost and iteration.

conceptChecks.question: When should document permissions be enforced?
options: Before retrieved content enters model context
conceptChecks.explanation: Retrieval is itself a data-access boundary.

conceptChecks.question: A high similarity score proves what?
options: Only that the configured similarity function ranked it highly
The user can edit the document
conceptChecks.explanation: Ranking is not an accuracy or authorization guarantee.

chapters.title: Ship SaaS features with an AI pair programmer
chapters.summary: Turn a request into a tested, observable release.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Work from a vertical slice
A small feature that spans sign-in, authorization, persistence and UI is more useful than several disconnected mock screens. Define the data contract first, then implement one complete user journey. Keep the existing app's database, authentication provider and deployment layout unless the task explicitly requires a migration.

## Control cost and failure
Put model calls behind a server boundary with timeouts, request limits and a budget. Keep provider keys out of browser bundles. A graceful fallback should preserve truthful state: do not display a locally simulated result as a saved server result. Record useful error categories without logging private prompts or tokens.

## Release deliberately
Use a feature branch and reviewable PR. Run tests and a production build, check migrations on an isolated database, and verify the deployed route. A successful build cannot tell you whether a production environment variable is missing. Observe latency and failure rates after release and keep a rollback path.

## Engineering exercise
Design an AI ticket-summary feature with a redacted input, request quota, deterministic test double, timeout response and user-visible retry. Define what data may be retained and which action still needs a human decision.

const result = { source: "local-preview", saved: false };
console.log(result.saved ? "Saved" : "Preview only");

keyTakeaways: Keep keys and privileged tools on the server.
Never label local fallback as verified persistence.
Validate migrations and deployed behavior.

title: Modern Java 21 & Spring Boot Architecture
subtitle: Model domains, manage concurrency and secure enterprise APIs.

chapters.title: JVM, records, sealed types & pattern matching
chapters.summary: Model domain values and handle explicit alternatives.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Separate language and runtime concepts
Java source is compiled to bytecode that runs on a JVM. Runtime optimization and garbage collection help execute programs, but they do not remove the need to profile allocation and latency. A memory leak can still occur when a long-lived reference retains objects the application no longer needs.

## Model data deliberately
A record provides a concise data carrier with component accessors and generated value-oriented methods. Its components are final references, not a guarantee of deep immutability. Defensively copy a mutable collection when your API requires an immutable snapshot.

## Make alternatives explicit
A sealed type constrains its permitted direct implementations. Pattern matching can make handling alternatives clearer. In Java 21, record patterns and pattern matching for switch are permanent features; do not assume every feature demonstrated in a preview article is enabled in a normal Java 21 build.

## Engineering exercise
Model a ticket lookup result as found or missing. Handle both states explicitly and test the missing branch. Prefer a domain result over a magic string that callers must remember to compare.
keyTakeaways: Records are not automatically deeply immutable.
Sealed types make allowed alternatives explicit.
Distinguish Java 21 final features from previews.

conceptChecks.question: What is a record component containing a mutable list?
options: A final reference that may still refer to mutable data
conceptChecks.explanation: The reference is final, but the referenced object can remain mutable.

conceptChecks.question: What can retain otherwise unused objects?
conceptChecks.explanation: Objects reachable through retained references cannot be reclaimed merely because the app no longer wants them.

chapters.title: Collections, streams & lambda expressions
chapters.summary: Build readable transformations without hidden mutation.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Choose collections by behavior
A List represents a sequence, a Set represents distinct elements, and a Map associates keys with values. The interface does not by itself define thread safety. Document ordering and mutability in an API instead of relying on a particular implementation by accident.

## Streams describe a pipeline
Intermediate operations such as filter and map describe transformations. A terminal operation consumes the pipeline. Prefer stateless functions; mutating an external counter or collection inside a stream can make ordering and parallel execution surprising. A stream is not a reusable collection.

## Parallel is not automatically faster
Parallel streams introduce scheduling and coordination costs. They are often a poor fit for blocking remote calls or operations requiring transaction context. Measure representative workloads and keep error handling explicit. A simple loop is a valid engineering choice when it communicates the operation better.

## Engineering exercise
Take a list of ticket priorities, retain urgent tickets and produce a new list. Verify the input is unchanged. Add duplicate values and explain whether they should be preserved or removed before choosing List or Set for the output.
keyTakeaways: Streams need a terminal operation.
Avoid shared mutable state in stream operations.
Measure before enabling parallel execution.

conceptChecks.question: Which operation consumes a stream pipeline?
options: A terminal operation such as toList
conceptChecks.explanation: Intermediate operations describe work; a terminal operation consumes the stream.

conceptChecks.question: Are all List implementations thread-safe?
options: Only when the variable uses var
conceptChecks.explanation: The List interface does not guarantee thread safety.

chapters.title: Virtual threads & CompletableFuture
chapters.summary: Use concurrency to wait efficiently without overwhelming dependencies.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Waiting is different from computing
Virtual threads in Java 21 make a thread-per-task style economical for many blocking workloads. They do not turn CPU-bound work into unlimited parallel processing. CPU capacity, database connections and remote-service rate limits still constrain throughput.

## Protect scarce resources
Use a semaphore or another admission-control mechanism to limit simultaneous calls to a database or vendor API. Creating more waiting tasks than a dependency can serve increases latency and memory pressure. Set timeouts and decide how cancellation propagates.

## Compose asynchronous work deliberately
CompletableFuture supports result composition and error handling. Distinguish thenApply, which maps a result, from thenCompose, which flattens a future-returning operation. Know which executor executes a stage, especially if it blocks. Always define a failure path rather than calling join at an arbitrary request boundary without a timeout strategy.

## Engineering exercise
Build a small fan-out service that queries two dependencies. Specify a concurrency limit, per-call timeout and partial-failure policy. Test that exceeding the limit queues or rejects work predictably instead of opening unbounded connections.
keyTakeaways: Virtual threads do not create more CPU or database capacity.
Use admission control for scarce dependencies.
Define timeout, executor and failure behavior.

conceptChecks.question: Which workload often benefits from virtual threads?
options: Many tasks waiting on blocking I/O
conceptChecks.explanation: Virtual threads are useful for high concurrency involving waiting.

conceptChecks.question: Which method flattens a stage that returns another future?
conceptChecks.explanation: thenCompose composes a future-returning asynchronous step.

chapters.title: Spring Boot 3, dependency injection & persistence
chapters.summary: Keep controllers, domain services and repositories distinct.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Follow a clear request path
A controller receives an HTTP request and translates it to a service operation. The service owns business rules, while repositories handle persistence. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and permits focused tests. Avoid coupling a domain decision to servlet request objects when a plain input object would suffice.

## Transactions protect a unit of work
A transaction boundary should surround the business operation that must succeed or fail together. Know how your framework applies transaction proxies; an internal self-call may not pass through the same interceptor. Do not assume that annotating an arbitrary private helper makes every caller transactional.

## JPA is not a query optimizer
Entity navigation can cause many additional queries, especially when serializing a collection of lazily loaded relationships. Inspect query counts and use explicit fetching or projections for the view you need. Do not serialize every entity field directly to clients, particularly credentials or internal authorization data.

## Engineering exercise
Design an assignment operation that validates the caller, checks a ticket's current state and records an audit event within one transaction. Return a DTO with only the allowed fields and test a concurrent reassignment.
keyTakeaways: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit.
Use DTOs instead of exposing entire entities.
Measure query counts to catch N+1 behavior.

conceptChecks.question: Which layer usually owns a business transaction?
conceptChecks.explanation: The transaction should enclose the business unit of work.

conceptChecks.question: What is a common N+1 symptom?
options: One query for each related row after the initial list query
conceptChecks.explanation: Lazy relationship access can produce an additional query per item.

chapters.title: JWT/OAuth2 security & Docker deployment
chapters.summary: Authorize each operation and make the runtime reproducible.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Verify tokens before trusting claims
A bearer token is a credential. Validate the signature with trusted keys and check the issuer, audience and expiry expected by the service. Decoding a token without verification does not establish identity. OAuth2 access and OpenID Connect identity concepts serve different purposes; use the appropriate token at each boundary.

## Authorization belongs beside the resource
After authenticating the caller, check tenant and role permissions for the requested entity. A valid token does not grant access to every ticket. Do not accept a role, owner ID or approved-email list supplied by the browser as proof of privilege.

## Build a constrained runtime
Use a repeatable image build and run the application with the least privileges it needs. Inject secrets at runtime, configure health checks, and define graceful shutdown. Containers do not automatically validate configuration or guarantee isolation from every dependency. Scan dependencies and test the image's actual startup command.

## Engineering exercise
Trace a request from gateway to controller to a tenant-scoped repository query. Define what the API returns for expired credentials, a forbidden tenant and a missing resource. Then document how to roll back a deployment without rolling back unrelated data.
keyTakeaways: Verify token signatures and expected claims.
Scope resource reads and writes to permitted tenants.
Inject secrets at runtime and test container startup.

conceptChecks.question: Is decoding a JWT enough to trust its claims?
options: No; verify its signature and expected claims
Only if its payload looks correct
Only when sent from a browser
conceptChecks.explanation: Unverified claims can be forged.

conceptChecks.question: What must happen after authentication?
options: Authorize access to the requested resource
conceptChecks.explanation: Identity and resource authorization are separate checks.

finalExamQuestions.question: What is a record component containing a mutable list?

chapters.title: Leakage-safe workflows & ColumnTransformer pipelines
chapters.summary: A useful model begins with a prediction contract: what decision is being made, at what moment, and which features are actually available then? Split data before fitting preprocessing.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Core concepts

A useful model begins with a prediction contract: what decision is being made, at what moment, and which features are actually available then? Split data before fitting preprocessing. A ColumnTransformer applies distinct transformations to numeric and categorical columns; a Pipeline keeps learned transformations inside the training workflow. A suspiciously high validation score can reflect leakage rather than a useful signal.

## Apply the workflow

For incident classification, group related incidents or customers before splitting when records are dependent. Fit imputers, scalers and encoders only on each training fold. Preserve column names and validate types at inference. Include an unknown-category policy and an explicit missing-value strategy. Evaluate a trivial baseline before investing in model complexity.

| Stage | Action | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Split | Respect groups/time and reserve the final test set | No entity or future event crosses the boundary |
| Fit | Fit transformations and estimator inside each CV fold | Fold scores, pipeline parameters and seed recorded |
| Serve | Validate feature schema and monitor drift/latency | Artifact revision and a rollback target are known |

> Common pitfall: Fitting a scaler on all rows exposes held-out distribution information. A pipeline does not fix a wrongly chosen split or a feature created after the target event.

Record one failure case and the evidence you would need before using this pattern in production. Code previews show the authored expected output; live model responses and platform reports can vary.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = pd.DataFrame({"age": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8],
                  "team": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"]})
y = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]
train, test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=7)
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", StandardScaler(), ["age"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["team"])])
model = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("clf", LogisticRegression())])
model.fit(train, y_train)
print(model.predict(test).shape)
print(list(model.named_steps))

## Core concepts

Regularization constrains how strongly a fitted model can adapt to its training data. A linear baseline is cheap to inspect and often competitive. Random forests average diverse trees; histogram gradient boosting builds successive corrections using binned features. Compare candidate families under the same evaluation protocol rather than assuming an ensemble always wins.

## Apply the workflow

Track training and validation performance together. If training improves while validation deteriorates, examine model capacity, leakage and sample size. Search a modest parameter space first and record random seeds, library versions and feature definitions. Choose latency, memory and calibration requirements before declaring the highest raw accuracy the winner.

chapters.summary: Clustering assigns structure without target labels, but a geometric cluster is not automatically a meaningful business segment.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Core concepts

Clustering assigns structure without target labels, but a geometric cluster is not automatically a meaningful business segment. K-Means prefers compact groups around centroids. DBSCAN groups dense regions and can identify noise. Feature scaling and distance choice strongly affect both methods. PCA finds directions of high variance, not necessarily the features most useful for a downstream decision.

## Apply the workflow

Inspect clusters with representative records and domain experts. Compare different scales and stability across resamples. Fit PCA within the training workflow if it precedes a predictive model. Decide how new observations will be handled: not every clustering estimator offers a direct predict method. Keep sensitive attributes out unless their use is justified and reviewed.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Split | Respect groups/time and reserve the final test set | No entity or future event crosses the boundary |
| Fit | Fit transformations and estimator inside each CV fold | Fold scores, pipeline parameters and seed recorded |
| Serve | Validate feature schema and monitor drift/latency | Artifact revision and a rollback target are known |

> Common pitfall: Choosing cluster count from a single attractive plot can conceal unstable or irrelevant segmentation. High variance is not synonymous with causal importance.

chapters.summary: Match a metric to the cost of errors.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Core concepts

Match a metric to the cost of errors. Precision asks how often positive predictions are correct; recall asks how many true positives are found. Precision-recall views are useful for rare positive outcomes. ROC-AUC evaluates ranking across thresholds, while a deployed threshold must still reflect operational costs. No single metric replaces an error analysis by meaningful subgroup.

## Apply the workflow

Use StratifiedKFold for suitable independent classification rows, but choose grouped or temporal splits when the data demands it. GridSearchCV must wrap the whole preprocessing-and-model pipeline. Keep a final test set untouched by tuning and threshold selection. Report uncertainty and compare against a baseline under identical splits.

| Stage | Action | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Split | Respect groups/time and reserve the final test set | No entity or future event crosses the boundary |
| Fit | Fit transformations and estimator inside each CV fold | Fold scores, pipeline parameters and seed recorded |
| Serve | Validate feature schema and monitor drift/latency | Artifact revision and a rollback target are known |

> Common pitfall: Stratification preserves class proportions; it does not prevent the same customer or future information from crossing train and validation.

Record one failure case and the evidence you would need before using this pattern in production. Code previews show the authored expected output; live model responses and platform reports can vary.

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
train, test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=7)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=7)
search = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)),
    {"logisticregression__C": [0.1, 1.0]}, scoring="average_precision", cv=cv)
search.fit(train, y_train)
scores = search.predict_proba(test)[:, 1]
print(0 <= average_precision_score(y_test, scores) <= 1)
print(0 <= roc_auc_score(y_test, scores) <= 1)

## Core concepts

A deployable artifact includes more than weights: feature schema, preprocessing, dependency versions, evaluation evidence and an intended-use statement matter. joblib persistence is convenient for trusted Python artifacts, but loading an untrusted pickle-compatible artifact can execute code. ONNX can support portable inference when the estimator and preprocessing operators have compatible converters.

## Apply the workflow

Expose a FastAPI boundary that validates a request schema before prediction. Load a trusted artifact once per worker rather than per request. Compare exported runtime predictions against the reference model on representative examples. Add latency limits, schema mismatch errors and drift monitoring. Keep an earlier artifact available for rollback and never log raw confidential inputs by default.

| Stage | Action | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Split | Respect groups/time and reserve the final test set | No entity or future event crosses the boundary |
| Fit | Fit transformations and estimator inside each CV fold | Fold scores, pipeline parameters and seed recorded |
| Serve | Validate feature schema and monitor drift/latency | Artifact revision and a rollback target are known |

> Common pitfall: Not every scikit-learn pipeline converts cleanly to ONNX. Conversion success alone does not prove numerical parity or correct preprocessing.

## Practice exercise

Reproduce the example in an isolated environment. Change one input or configuration, predict the effect, then compare the observed behavior. Record one failure case and the evidence you would need before using this pattern in production. Code previews show the authored expected output; live model responses and platform reports can vary.

### ONNX and API release checklist

ONNX conversion is a deployment choice, not a universal serialization guarantee. Check converter support for every transformer and estimator before selecting it. Compare the original pipeline and the converted runtime on the same representative inputs, including missing values and unknown categories. Preserve feature ordering, data types and class labels. Reject malformed requests at the API boundary and include model revision in operational logs.

The example below trains a tiny tree, writes and reloads its own temporary artifact, then defines a typed FastAPI endpoint. It is an interface exercise rather than a production model. A real deployment also needs authentication, rate limits, dependency pinning, health probes and rollback testing. Keep the training and serving environment definitions together; do not accept untrusted serialized models.

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import joblib
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# Only load artifacts created by a trusted build, using matching dependencies.
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "model.joblib"
    joblib.dump(model, path)
    restored = joblib.load(path)

app = FastAPI()
class Features(BaseModel):
    value: float = Field(ge=0, le=1)

@app.post("/predict")
def predict(features: Features):
    return {"class": int(restored.predict([[features.value]])[0])}

print(predict(Features(value=1)))

## Core concepts

Short Python expressions help most when their behavior is obvious. Counter counts hashable values, defaultdict supplies missing values, and itertools supports lazy composition. Unpacking can clarify fixed-shape records. A short expression is not inherently faster or safer than a clear loop, so preserve the data contract and test empty input.

## Apply the workflow

Build a ticket-frequency report from normalized IDs. Decide whether order matters and whether case normalization is acceptable. Use an iterator for large input and materialize only the small summary. pathlib represents paths without manual separator concatenation. JSON and CSV parsers understand their own escaping rules, so avoid splitting records with ad hoc string operations. Build a log summarizer that opens text with a known encoding, iterates through lines and emits a compact count. Test malformed records and define whether to stop, skip with a counter or quarantine them. Resolve user-controlled paths against an approved directory before reading. chapters.summary: A context manager gives a resource a defined acquisition and cleanup boundary.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Core concepts

A context manager gives a resource a defined acquisition and cleanup boundary. Use it for files, locks and temporary state. lru_cache avoids repeated work for hashable inputs, but cached results are retained and may become stale. It is a poor default for user-specific authorization decisions unless scope and invalidation are designed explicitly.

## Apply the workflow

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Core concepts

AsyncIO coordinates tasks that yield while waiting. ThreadPoolExecutor can run suitable blocking I/O without blocking the event loop, but more workers do not create more downstream capacity. Retry only failures that are safe to repeat. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retry traffic; a maximum attempt count and deadline bound the damage.

## Apply the workflow

Use an idempotency key for operations with side effects and do not retry a forbidden request as if it were a transient outage. Propagate cancellation when the original request no longer needs the result.

| Inspect | Compare outputs and profile representative traffic | A measured change replaces a guessed optimization |

import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

async def retry(operation, attempts=3):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            return await operation()
        except TimeoutError:
            if attempt + 1 == attempts:
                raise
            await asyncio.sleep(min(0.01 * 2 ** attempt, 0.1))

    async def flaky():
        nonlocal calls
        calls += 1
        if calls < 2:
            raise TimeoutError("temporary")
        return "READY"
    print(await retry(flaky))
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        print(await asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor(pool, str.upper, "done"))
asyncio.run(main())

## Core concepts

## Apply the workflow

Estimate cost from measured token usage, apply per-request limits and support cancellation. Separate streamed display events from final saved state. LoRA learns low-rank updates to selected model weights rather than training every base parameter. Rank affects adapter capacity and parameter count; alpha participates in scaling under the selected implementation. Target modules depend on architecture. Copying module names from another model without inspecting the actual structure can silently change or break the intended adaptation.

## Apply the workflow

Inspect trainable parameter counts and verify that the expected modules receive adapters. Start with a small rank and a held-out evaluation before expanding capacity. Record the base model revision together with adapter configuration. Confirm the optimizer sees trainable adapter parameters and that inference loads the adapter against a compatible base.

QLoRA combines a quantized base model with trainable adapters. bitsandbytes configuration can request 4-bit loading, NF4 and nested quantization, with a separate compute dtype. Weight storage precision is not the same as compute precision. Training memory also includes activations, optimizer state, sequence length and runtime overhead.

## Apply the workflow

Estimate the complete workload before choosing a GPU. A 16 GB device may support some model and sequence configurations, but no universal fit guarantee follows from the phrase QLoRA.
